7c4c5f6e5932: The Seventh Tradition's Long Form says five things, in this order:
bb1ef3378e62: <0>Members pay.</0> The groups "ought to be fully supported by the voluntary contributions of their own members" (p. 564). In 1946 this was still a goal; the text says each group "should soon achieve this ideal" (p. 564).
a477784522ee: <0>No public appeals in A.A.'s name.</0> Public solicitation of funds using the A.A. name is "highly dangerous," whoever does it: groups, clubs, hospitals or outside agencies (p. 564).
3e028fbb4734: <0>No big gifts, and no strings.</0> Accepting "large gifts from any source," or contributions "carrying any obligation whatever," is unwise (p. 564). "Any source" includes members.
4d7f6cbc2046: <0>No hoarding.</0> It views "with much concern" group treasuries that keep accumulating money, beyond prudent reserves, for no stated A.A. purpose (p. 564).
c028a029cda5: <0>Why.</0> "Experience has often warned us that nothing can so surely destroy our spiritual heritage as futile disputes over property, money, and authority" (p. 564).
15e728c0abf9: The short form, "Every A.A. group ought to be fully self-supporting, declining outside contributions" (p. 562), condenses all of this into one line.
ab337a3ebbac: How it came about: Bill W.'s "Money" (1946)
7a2cf50a302d: <0>At first there was no money to argue about.</0> Members met in homes, and if one wanted to help another alcoholic financially, that was his own affair (P-17, p. 27). Bill accepts that this couldn't last: meeting places, clubs and offices cost money, so the real question was how to limit money so that it never topples the spiritual foundation (P-17, pp. 27–28).
8a631d0df6c0: <0>Members' contributions keep the services honest.</0> Contributions are never a condition of membership (P-17, p. 28). Because nobody is compelled to pay, A.A.'s offices "can never dictate" (P-17, "Money", 1946, p. 29): if they serve badly, members stop paying. That is why members' own voluntary contributions should be "eventually our sole support" (P-17, "Money", 1946, p. 32).
c2fa15809939: <0>A.A. did take outside help once, and says so.</0> There was a time "when we desperately needed a little outside aid" (P-17, "Money", 1946, p. 33). Friends' gifts made possible the Alcoholic Foundation, the book <1>Alcoholics Anonymous</1> and the General Office, and Bill writes that A.A. would never stop being grateful (P-17, p. 33).
ed0a1c4ee894: <0>Why that changed.</0> By 1946 A.A. had thousands of members earning a living, and a strong feeling spread that A.A. should support itself (P-17, p. 33). Let the public's money go to research, hospitals and education, which need it; "We can, and we should, pay our own way" (P-17, "Money", 1946, p. 34).
cda0b6d524f6: <0>What counts and what doesn't.</0> A nonalcoholic friend dropping a dollar in the hat is hardly an exception to self-support (P-17, p. 34). The concern is "the large contributions, especially those that may carry future obligations" (P-17, "Money", 1946, p. 34), and money left to A.A. in wills, public solicitation in A.A.'s name, and money from "wet" or "dry" sources, which would drag A.A. into the alcohol controversy (P-17, p. 34). Bill even questions a large gift from a wealthy member: might the group feel in his debt, and might he think he had bought his sobriety (P-17, p. 34)? His conclusion is that "acceptance of large donations from any source whatever is very questionable" (P-17, "Money", 1946, p. 34).
017cc2f198b3: <0>The trustees' decision.</0> Bill reports that the trustees of the Alcoholic Foundation had just resolved to turn down any gift carrying the slightest obligation and any earnings offered from a commercial source, including money from film companies interested in an A.A. film, because "A.A. has nothing to sell" (P-17, "Money", 1946, p. 35).

d7bf8fc6fa7f: How Bill W. worked it out in "Money" (1946)
4934a5dd74cc: <0>Why members worried.</0> Clubs and offices were hiring paid workers, and members feared a paid class would grow inside A.A. Bill says the fear was understandable: in A.A. every member is a volunteer missionary in his own right, so there is no need for anyone to be paid for simple Twelfth Step work, "a purely spiritual undertaking" (P-17, "Money", 1946, p. 30).
1dead803d821: <0>The line he drew.</0> "A janitor can sweep the floor, a cook can boil the beef," a steward can remove a troublesome drunk, a secretary can run an office, an editor can put out a paper, and none of that professionalizes A.A. (P-17, "Money", 1946, p. 30). If members didn't do these jobs, A.A. would have to hire nonalcoholics, and nobody expects a nonalcoholic to work full time for nothing (P-17, p. 30). If such a worker also does some Twelfth Step work along the way, that changes nothing. The principle: "we may pay well for special services — but never for straight Twelfth Step work" (P-17, "Money", 1946, p. 31).
628047068331: <0>What professionalizing would look like.</0> Bill gives his own example: a sign on an office door reading "Bill W. — Alcoholics Anonymous Therapist," with an hourly fee (P-17, p. 31). That would be treating alcoholics for money while trading on A.A.'s name, which he calls legal but "hardly ethical" (P-17, p. 31).
bd9cb7a7dc36: <0>Members who work in the field.</0> Bill doesn't condemn therapists, and doesn't bar members from the work. Trained social workers, psychologists and psychiatrists who are A.A. members shouldn't "feel excluded" (P-17, p. 31). What they must not do is advertise themselves as A.A. therapists or use their A.A. connection publicly; like a tennis player turning pro, they drop their amateur standing (P-17, p. 31). He goes on: members offered jobs as nurses, doctors, social workers, educators or personnel officers can take them, as long as they avoid "A.A. therapy" and anything that would hurt A.A. as a whole (P-17, pp. 32–33).
d3feaa136bce: His summary, point (f): A.A. must avoid professionalization at all costs; "simple Twelfth Step work is never to be paid for" (P-17, "Money", 1946, p. 32); members in alcohol therapy must never trade on their A.A. connection; and there can never be an "A.A. therapist." 18297b4ebc95: In "Dangers in Linking A.A. to Other Projects," Bill applies the same idea to members who work in hospitals, research or alcohol education. a2081b185585: The Ninth Tradition's Long Form walks through A.A.'s structure from the bottom up:
6222966647f0: <0>The group.</0> Each group "needs the least possible organization," and rotating leadership is best (p. 565). A small group may elect a secretary; a large one, a rotating committee (p. 565).
32ac1a9f5c6b: <0>The city.</0> The groups of a large metropolitan area may elect a central or intergroup committee, which often employs a full-time secretary (p. 565).
52739545861b: <0>New York.</0> The trustees "are, in effect, our A.A. General Service Committee" (p. 565). They look after the A.A. Tradition, receive the voluntary contributions that pay for the General Service Office, handle overall public relations because the groups have authorized them to, and guarantee the integrity of the Grapevine (p. 565).
1da151711899: <0>What all of them are.</0> Every such representative is to be guided by the spirit of service, "for true leaders in A.A. are but trusted and experienced servants of the whole" (p. 565). They have no real authority from their titles, "they do not govern," and "Universal respect is the key to their usefulness" (p. 565).
d0797bf90ca2: Two notes on wording. The Big Book prints "the trustees of the General Service Board"; the 1946 original said "The Alcoholic Foundation," which was renamed in 1954 (P-17, Foreword, 1955, p. 7). And the Long Form doesn't say A.A. "ought never be organized." That phrase is the short form's (p. 562). The Long Form says <0>the least possible</0> organization, and then names the organization A.A. has.
136edeec8f66: Bill W., "Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?" (1947)
4a3588281d2b: <0>His answer.</0> "The answer to this question is almost surely" no, and he says experience has settled it (P-17, "Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?", 1947, p. 37).
509517ff35e0: <0>Why.</0> Alcoholics could rarely govern themselves, and families, doctors, clergy and judges had failed to govern them by force (P-17, p. 37). But alcoholics can be led and inspired, so the only real authority in A.A. is spiritual principle: "It is never personal authority" (P-17, "Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?", 1947, p. 37). He lists what A.A. lacks: no fees, no dues, no rules, no demand that anyone conform, "no one set in personal authority over anyone else" (P-17, "Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?", 1947, p. 37).
181089843f2f: <0>Why groups follow the Traditions anyway.</0> Members follow the Steps by choice, because they prefer recovery to death: "We conform because we want to" (P-17, "Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?", 1947, p. 38). Groups follow the Twelve Points of Tradition for the same reason: they see they would fall apart if they didn't (P-17, p. 38).
0f1d8574117d: <0>No one can compel a group.</0> There is no constituted "human authority that can compel an A.A. group to do anything" (P-17, "Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?", 1947, p. 38). An elected leader can guide by example or persuasion but can never boss, or he is passed over at the next election (P-17, p. 38). Rotating committees "have only the authorization to serve, never to command" (P-17, "Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?", 1947, p. 38); each carries out what it thinks its group wants. Committees that tried to discipline members or police their morals achieved nothing lasting, except perhaps getting a new committee elected (P-17, p. 38).
a7c49dbc4f2c: <0>Bill's own attempt.</0> He tried to govern A.A. himself, and each time "I have been shouted down" (P-17, "Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?", 1947, p. 39). Personal power always failed, and he concluded that in A.A. "one can be a servant only" (P-17, "Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?", 1947, p. 39).
200b1dca171c: <0>The center is a center of service.</0> The General Office supplies information and literature, helps new groups when asked, looks after public relations and sometimes mediates (P-17, p. 39). The Grapevine's editors see themselves as a mirror of A.A., unable to rule or propagandize, and the trustees are "caretakers only" (P-17, "Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?", 1947, p. 39). Even at the center there are only custodians, editors and secretaries, none with authority to govern A.A. (P-17, p. 39). So long as A.A. avoids piling up wealth or personal government at these centers, he writes, it can't go astray (P-17, pp. 39–40).
0d0cd80f9e25: It settles that no person, committee, office or board in A.A. has authority over a group or a member. It doesn't say A.A. has no structure: the Long Form names the structure and explains whom it answers to. For how a group's own decisions are reached, see <0>Is group conscience a majority vote?</0> and <1>Tradition Two: does anyone have authority in A.A.?</1>

35dbf6b3934d: The dates, from the books themselves
00d4e2612482: <0>1939: the Steps.</0> The Twelve Steps are in Chapter 5, "How It Works" (pp. 59–60), part of the first edition, whose first printing was in 1939 (p. xiii). The 1939 book has no Traditions. The nearest thing is a few lines in the Foreword to the First Edition: no fees or dues, "The only requirement for membership is an honest desire to stop drinking," no alliance with any sect, and a request that members stay anonymous in the press (pp. xiii–xiv).
c7e85cb26d67: <0>1946: the Long Form.</0> The Big Book's own appendix calls the short form "a condensed version of the original 'long form' A.A. Traditions as first printed in 1946" (p. 561). Bill W. dates it to "the Grapevine of May, 1946" (<1>A.A. Comes of Age</1>, 1957), with more Grapevine pieces explaining each point over the following months. Those essays, from 1946 and 1947, are reprinted in the pamphlet P-17.
2bddc13d6515: <0>About 1947–1950: the short form.</0> Bill credits Earl T., founder of the Chicago group, with the idea of cutting the Long Form down to statements as short as the Steps. Earl came to him with it "One day in 1947, or thereabouts" (<1>A.A. Comes of Age</1>, 1957). After months of refining, the Grapevine printed the new wording in every issue.
e5770aad7d3a: <0>1950: confirmed at Cleveland.</0> The Foreword to the Second Edition (1955) says the principles "had become so widely accepted by 1950 that they were confirmed by our first International Conference held at Cleveland" (p. xix). Bill puts it in July 1950 and records the Convention's "unanimous voice of consent" (<1>A.A. Comes of Age</1>, 1957).
b80ce8908ce0: So the Steps came first by seven years, and the Traditions in their familiar form came about eleven years after the Steps.
1db840a306fc: The Traditions grew out of problems that didn't exist in 1939. When the Big Book came out, A.A. was "more than one hundred men and women" (p. xiii). By the close of 1941 it was about 8,000 (p. xviii). Then came what the Second Edition foreword calls a "fearsome and exciting adolescent period" (p. xviii), with quarrels over membership, leadership and money (pp. xviii–xix). The Traditions were the lessons drawn from those years (see <0>Why were the Twelve Traditions written?</0>).
1959cab54724: Bill described the order in which things happened: "Nobody invented Alcoholics Anonymous. It grew." (P-17, Foreword, 1955). Lessons were adopted "first as policy and then as tradition" (P-17, Foreword, 1955).
384bc00345ac: Bill himself compared them. In the foreword to P-17 he wrote that many members already felt "we ought to apply them as seriously to our group life as we do the Twelve Recovery Steps" (P-17, Foreword, 1955) to each member's own life. He added: "Of this, it will take time to tell." In 1947 he wrote that groups follow the Traditions "for the very same reason that the individual A.A. follows the Twelve Steps to recovery" (P-17, "Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?", 1947). By 1957 he could write that, a few years after 1946, the Traditions were seen to be as necessary to the society as the Steps were to each member, and "the key to the unity, the functioning, and even the survival" of A.A. (<0>A.A. Comes of Age</0>, 1957). At first, though, many members found them a bore.
2209aea089f6: A later pamphlet (P-43, 1971) makes the same point about how both were made: "Like the Steps, the Traditions were not figured out in advance" (P-43, 1971).

720c5027a6b0: No. The Big Book introduces the Traditions as A.A.'s best answers to two life-or-death questions: how A.A. can best function, and how it can stay whole and survive (p. 561). Without unity, it says, "most of us will finally die alone" (p. 561).
c25e5b54f865: The Traditions record things that had already gone wrong: membership rules that would have kept out nine-tenths of the early members, groups that went into the hospital business, fights over money and clubs, members who used A.A.'s name for their own causes.
ef19db76990a: They aren't rules either. In 1955 the Big Book said none of them had "the force of rules or laws" (p. xix), and Bill W. warned that if A.A. hardened them, "the letter might crush that spirit." Groups follow them by choice, for the same reason members follow the Steps.
65d7380e2f17: What the Big Book says they are for (Appendix I)
af166bc7f372: Appendix I opens by saying what's at stake. A.A. has made "the difference between misery and sobriety, and often the difference between life and death" for its members, and could mean as much to alcoholics not yet reached (p. 561). So no society ever had a more urgent need for lasting unity: "We alcoholics see that we must work together and hang together, else most of us will finally die alone" (p. 561). The Traditions are "the best answers that our experience has yet given" to how A.A. can best function and stay whole (p. 561).
b4c1e5b5f425: The Long Form starts from the same place. Each member is a small part of a great whole, and "A.A. must continue to live or most of us will surely die" (p. 563). Its Seventh Tradition gives the reason behind several of the others: "Experience has often warned us that nothing can so surely destroy our spiritual heritage as futile disputes over property, money, and authority" (p. 564).
d55b2fb17edd: Where they came from: experience, not theory
c7d6ae05cdb0: Bill W.'s essays from 1946–47 show the Traditions growing out of trouble:
1b48d93077b9: <0>Membership.</0> When the office collected the groups' membership rules, Bill found that if all of them had been enforced, "it would have been practically impossible for any alcoholic" to join; about nine-tenths of the oldest members would never have got in (P-17, "Who Is a Member of Alcoholics Anonymous?", 1946, p. 11).
c4d634e57be1: <0>Hospitals and business.</0> Groups that ran their own drying-out places found it put them into business, and it almost always backfired (P-17, p. 15).
4dcd288f408e: <0>Clubs.</0> New York's first club tangled the groups, the club and the area's money for years (P-17, pp. 19–20).
47b8a4bedc67: <0>Money.</0> Bill saw "the great ordeal of its own prosperity and success" as A.A.'s supreme test (P-17, "Money", 1946, p. 35).
e9f3a9a7e1c7: <0>Authority.</0> Every time Bill tried to govern A.A. himself, he was "shouted down" (P-17, p. 39).
ed20c5add5ff: The Big Book's 1955 foreword sums it up: as A.A. grew, it faced the very problems feared, over money, power and splits, "in every group" (p. xix). Out of that came the conviction that A.A. had to unify or die (p. xix).
58b712c885de: How seriously Bill meant them (P-17 foreword, 1955)
93832f3d945d: Unity doesn't look after itself. Like personal recovery, A.A. would always have to work at it, with honesty, humility and "above all — vigilance" (P-17, Foreword, 1955, p. 5). Bill asks every member to be as aware of what endangers A.A. as of his own defects, "For whole movements have, before now, gone on benders, too!" (P-17, Foreword, 1955, p. 5).
be29fe994b7a: He calls the Twelve Points "our first attempt to state sound principles of group conduct and public relations" (P-17, Foreword, 1955, p. 5), and reports that many members felt "we ought to apply them as seriously to our group life as we do the Twelve Recovery Steps" to themselves (P-17, Foreword, 1955, p. 5).
db472bb01e34: In the same foreword Bill warns against the opposite mistake. "Nobody invented Alcoholics Anonymous. It grew" (P-17, Foreword, 1955, p. 5). Experience became policy, then tradition, and he hoped that process would never stop. "Should we ever harden too much, the letter might crush that spirit" (P-17, Foreword, 1955, p. 5). A.A. could victimize itself "by petty rules and prohibitions" or ask alcoholics to accept rigid ideas or stay away (P-17, Foreword, 1955, p. 5). "Yet the lessons of our experience count for a great deal" (P-17, Foreword, 1955, p. 5).
637cf80e4373: In 1947 he explained why groups keep them without anyone enforcing them. Members follow the Steps from choice because they prefer recovery to death; groups follow the Traditions "for the very same reason," because they see "they would disintegrate if they didn't" (P-17, "Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?", 1947, p. 38).
23e533da2d22: The Big Book's 1955 foreword adds that though none of the principles had the force of rules or laws, they were so widely accepted by 1950 that A.A.'s first International Conference, held at Cleveland, confirmed them (p. xix).
b97b3fffb9ed: The Traditions aren't decoration and aren't red tape. They're A.A.'s record of how groups nearly destroyed themselves, written down so newer groups don't have to learn it the same way. They also aren't laws: nobody can enforce them, and Bill feared what would happen if anyone tried. A group that reads only the one-line short forms misses most of that history. The Long Form and Bill's essays keep the reasons attached. See <0>What is the Long Form, and why read it instead of the short form?</0>

ef6fc7452de7: The Long Form is the original wording of the Twelve Traditions, first printed in the A.A. Grapevine in 1946. The short form, which the Big Book calls "the form in general use today" (p. 561), is a condensed version made from it a few years later.
ad9f6bc39199: The Big Book prints both, in Appendix I: the short form on page 562 and the Long Form on pages 563–566. It says the Long Form is "more explicit" (p. 561).
16b6251326fc: The short form drops a great deal: who a group may refuse (no one), what counts as a group, how clubs and hospitals must be set apart from the groups (hospitals "well outside A.A."), what professionalism means, and more. Reading only the short form, you miss much of what the Traditions actually say.
5ff028bf1188: Appendix I calls the short form "a condensed version of the original 'long form' A.A. Traditions as first printed in 1946" (p. 561). Bill W. published those original twelve points as "Twelve Points to Assure Our Future" (P-17, Foreword, 1955), and explained them in a series of Grapevine essays in 1946 and 1947, now reprinted in the pamphlet P-17.
ff28ae36c9d9: The short form came later. Bill says the idea of cutting the Long Form down to the length of the Steps came from Earl T. of Chicago "in 1947, or thereabouts" (<0>A.A. Comes of Age</0>, 1957). The Traditions were confirmed at Cleveland in 1950 (p. xix), and Bill says they had already been cut down to the short form by then (<1>A.A. Comes of Age</1>, 1957).
15351357bda3: P-17's introduction says plainly what happened to the wording. "In all but the Second Tradition" (P-17, introduction), it says, the original language was changed or shortened.
e76bb97749fe: What the short form leaves out
d80b38d79862: Laid side by side, the Long Form says much more. Some of the biggest differences:
165f56c09020: <0>One.</0> The short form says the common welfare comes first. The Long Form says why (each member is "but a small part of a great whole," and A.A. must live or most of us will die) and adds a line the short form drops: "But individual welfare follows close afterward" (p. 563).
c64114af7fa6: <0>Three.</0> The short form gives the one requirement for membership. The Long Form says A.A. should include all who suffer from alcoholism, "Hence we may refuse none who wish to recover" (p. 563), that membership should never depend on "money or conformity" (p. 563), and that any two or three alcoholics gathered for sobriety may call themselves a group, "provided that, as a group, they have no other affiliation" (p. 563). The definition of an A.A. group, and its ban on outside affiliation, are only in the Long Form.
a4149bb8b053: <0>Four.</0> The short form says groups are autonomous except where others are affected. The Long Form spells out the exceptions: consult neighbouring groups when your plans affect them, and confer with the trustees before any action that might greatly affect A.A. as a whole (p. 563).
9e1e75d404aa: <0>Six.</0> The short form is one sentence about endorsing, financing or lending the A.A. name. The Long Form is a full paragraph: property should be separately incorporated, "thus dividing the material from the spiritual" (p. 564); a group "should never go into business" (p. 564); clubs and hospitals should be set apart so the groups can drop them; hospitals belong "well outside A.A.—and medically supervised" (p. 564); and a group "can bind itself to no one" (p. 564).
c20a9ccd2db2: <0>Seven.</0> The Long Form warns against public fundraising in A.A.'s name, large gifts, gifts with strings, and treasuries that pile up money "for no stated A.A. purpose" (p. 564).
7e8964defd53: <0>Eight.</0> Only the Long Form defines professionalism: "the occupation of counseling alcoholics for fees or hire" (p. 564).
4c086cd2c2ee: <0>Nine.</0> The Long Form describes rotating leadership and says leaders "derive no real authority from their titles; they do not govern" (p. 565). The short form moved "they do not govern" into Tradition Two.
b8e4bfba955d: <0>Ten.</0> The Long Form names the outside issues: "politics, alcohol reform, or sectarian religion" (p. 565), and says the groups "oppose no one" (p. 565).
fcdfb053be05: <0>Eleven.</0> Only the Long Form says: "There is never need to praise ourselves" (p. 565).
d8e9a5d22a78: <0>Twelve.</0> The Long Form says anonymity means practising "a genuine humility" (p. 566).
b096d48a1507: Two, the one Tradition P-17 says kept its original language, is the same sentence in both forms; the short form adds the "trusted servants" line from Nine (pp. 562–563).
c49d3f8a7b0d: Two printings of the Long Form
e11ed5a7c7a3: The Long Form in the Big Book and the one in P-17 are almost word for word the same, with small updates. In P-17, Tradition Four tells groups to confer with "the trustees of The Alcoholic Foundation" (P-17, Foreword, 1955), with a footnote that the Foundation was renamed the General Service Board in 1954. The Big Book's printing says "the trustees of the General Service Board" (p. 563). P-17's Tradition Three reads "all who suffer alcoholism," where the Big Book has "all who suffer from alcoholism" (p. 563). Neither change alters the meaning, but it's worth knowing that the Big Book copy has been brought up to date.
fa47c5f198ee: A short summary is easy to quote and easy to bend. "Each group should be autonomous" can be made to sound as if a group can do anything, until you read the Long Form's limits. "An A.A. group ought never endorse..." can sound like a narrow rule about logos, until you read a paragraph that keeps hospitals outside A.A. altogether. The Long Form is the fuller statement, and the Big Book reprints it for that reason.

c7931a6b541c: They aren't rules in the sense of laws someone can enforce. The Big Book says "none of these principles had the force of rules or laws" (p. xix), and no one in A.A. has the power to make a group obey them.

25a86b042eab: Most of the Traditions speak to A.A. groups and to A.A. as a whole. But several also speak to members when they act as A.A. members or could implicate A.A.: in public, in the press, and when money is involved.

b918bb758803: Not rules: what the books say
34527dd983a5: The Foreword to the Second Edition (1955) says it directly: "Though none of these principles had the force of rules or laws, they had become so widely accepted by 1950 that they were confirmed" at Cleveland (p. xix).
2cc10561b0d4: Introducing the original Twelve Points, Bill W. called them "these suggestions" (P-17, Foreword, 1955) for a tradition of relations, and asked whether they could grow into traditions held "by his own deep conviction and by the common consent of his fellows" (P-17, Foreword, 1955). Looking back in 1957, he wrote that a code of traditions "could not, of course, ever become rule or law" (<0>A.A. Comes of Age</0>, 1957), but could guide the trustees, the New York office, and "especially" groups with growing pains.
e560e5ffbb9a: Bill's 1947 essay on authority explains why there's no one to enforce them. Nowhere in A.A., he wrote, is there any human authority that "can compel an A.A. group to do anything" (P-17, "Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?", 1947). Groups follow the Traditions for the same reason members follow the Steps: "Groups see they would disintegrate if they didn't" (P-17, "Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?", 1947).
f8b23e7b3786: He also warned against turning them into a rulebook: "We could victimize ourselves by petty rules and prohibitions" (P-17, Foreword, 1955).
f238b80c0cdc: The Long Form opens "Our A.A. experience has taught us that:" (p. 563). Its language is "ought" and "should," and in places "never": - "An A.A. group, as such, should never go into business" (p. 564). - Cooperation with outsiders "ought never go so far as affiliation or endorsement, actual or implied" (p. 564). - "Alcoholics Anonymous should remain forever nonprofessional" (p. 564).
f9f58d6e8a4c: Bill's essays explain each "never" with what went wrong when groups tried otherwise (see <0>Why were the Twelve Traditions written?</0>). So the honest answer is: unenforced, but firm.
84ad9e4b3266: <0>Groups and A.A. as a whole, mainly.</0> Appendix I says they answer "How can A.A. best function?" and "How can A.A. best stay whole and so survive?" (p. 561). The Long Form keeps addressing "each A.A. group" (pp. 563–565). Tradition Two is "For our group purpose" (p. 563). Tradition Four is about each group's own affairs (p. 563). Five, Six and Seven are about what a group is for, what it may get involved in, and how it pays its way (pp. 563–564). Nine is about how groups and their service boards are organized (p. 565).
18116ec450cf: <0>Members too, where A.A. is involved.</0> The Long Form doesn't leave the individual out: - One starts with the member: "Each member of Alcoholics Anonymous is but a small part of a great whole" (p. 563). - Eight says counseling alcoholics for fees is professionalism, and that ordinary Twelfth Step work is never to be paid for (pp. 564–565). That's work members do. - Ten: "No A.A. group or member should ever, in such a way as to implicate A.A., express any opinion on outside controversial issues" (p. 565). - Eleven: "Our names and pictures as A.A. members ought not be broadcast, filmed, or publicly printed" (p. 565).
0ab864ccf538: The line the texts draw is where A.A. is involved. Bill's 1947 essay on outside projects says members are free to work in other fields "if they act as individuals only, and are careful of the A.A. name" (P-17, "Dangers in Linking A.A. to Other Projects", 1947). In 1957 he wrote that the Traditions "ask for personal as well as group sacrifice" (<0>A.A. Comes of Age</0>, 1957), including never to use the A.A. name for personal power, distinction or money.
9ed31337c198: So "the Steps are for members, the Traditions are for groups" is only half right. The Traditions are about A.A.'s unity, and a member acting as an A.A., or speaking publicly as one, is inside that.
e94f2e17cd19: Nothing in the Long Form governs people or organizations outside A.A. It tells A.A. groups to keep outside enterprises at a distance, and says the management of clubs and hospitals "should be the sole responsibility of those people who financially support them" (p. 564). The Long Form does say public fundraising in A.A.'s name is "highly dangerous" even when done by "other outside agencies" (p. 564), but that is A.A. stating its concern, not a rule anyone outside can be held to. A hospital, a treatment centre or an independent website isn't bound by A.A.'s Traditions; an A.A. group's relationship with it is.
e4067c6c181e: A later pamphlet says the same thing about rules and members: "the Traditions are not rules — and they are not just for officers" (P-43, 1971). The A.A. group pamphlet (P-16, 2018) quotes the 1962 Twelve Concepts: "no penalties to be inflicted for nonconformity to A.A. principles" (P-16, 2018).

ff1947d8675e: The Traditions were written to keep A.A. alive and in one piece. The Big Book says they answer two questions: "How can A.A. best function?" and "How can A.A. best stay whole and so survive?" (p. 561).
b796c75274ba: They came out of real trouble in the 1940s, as A.A. grew from about a hundred members to many thousands: fights over membership, leadership, money, property and publicity.
95a93f2bd080: Bill W. put the lessons into words and published them in the A.A. Grapevine in 1946. He said he hadn't invented them; the groups had learned them the hard way.
beba78bf1612: The reason given is survival, for the members as much as for A.A.: "A.A. must continue to live or most of us will surely die" (p. 563).
43320aa29801: Appendix I, "The A.A. Tradition," opens by saying A.A. has made the difference between misery and sobriety, often between life and death, for those in it, and could do the same for alcoholics not yet reached (p. 561). So no society ever had "a more urgent need for continuous effectiveness and permanent unity" (p. 561). Alcoholics have to "work together and hang together" or most will "die alone" (p. 561).
8cd82af321be: The Long Form itself opens with the words "Our A.A. experience has taught us that:" (p. 563). Each Tradition is stated as something experience taught, not as a plan worked out in advance.
41ec0de53c88: The Foreword to the Second Edition (1955) tells the same story in brief. After the publicity of 1939–1941, A.A. entered an "adolescent period" (p. xviii). Could thousands of alcoholics meet and work together? Would there be quarrels over membership, leadership and money, or splits that broke A.A. apart (pp. xviii–xix)? The answer that grew out of it was that "A.A.'s had to hang together or die separately" (p. xix). Just as the Steps were principles an alcoholic could live by, the groups and A.A. as a whole needed principles to "survive and function effectively" (p. xix).
f5aa23f6b222: What Bill W. said when he wrote them (1946–1947)
77db99f2779f: Bill's introduction to the original "Twelve Points to Assure Our Future" is printed in the pamphlet P-17. "Almost any A.A. can tell you what our group problems are," he wrote (P-17, Foreword, 1955). They were about the member's relation to his group, the group's relation to A.A. as a whole, and A.A.'s place in the world outside, and above all about leadership, money and authority. He asked whether A.A. had enough experience yet to state principles "which could grow into vital traditions" (P-17, Foreword, 1955), and offered the Twelve Points as his attempt. (The pamphlet dates its whole foreword 1955, though this part introduces the 1946 Points, so we date it 1955.)
c453b0385487: His 1946–47 Grapevine essays fill in the troubles behind each point: - <0>Membership.</0> Groups had written so many membership rules that, if all had been enforced at once, almost no alcoholic could have joined (P-17, "Who Is a Member of Alcoholics Anonymous?", 1946). - <1>Money and property.</1> Groups that set up their own drying-out places, or raised money from the public in A.A.'s name, ran into trouble, and disputes over money threatened what A.A. was for (P-17, "Money", 1946; "Hospitals and A.A.", 1947). - <2>Outside causes.</2> Members wanted A.A. to put its name behind education, research and reform (P-17, "Dangers in Linking A.A. to Other Projects", 1947). - <3>Authority.</3> Committees and old-timers, Bill included, tried to run things and failed (P-17, "Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?", 1947).
a66ba66e5edf: He also said why groups would keep them without anyone enforcing them: "Groups see they would disintegrate if they didn't" (P-17, "Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?", 1947).
c727d0299a52: How they were put on paper (1957 account)
847ddafb0299: In <0>A.A. Comes of Age</0> (1957), Bill gives the history. Letters about group problems poured into the New York office, and "The basic ideas for the Twelve Traditions of Alcoholics Anonymous came directly out of this vast correspondence" (<1>A.A. Comes of Age</1>, 1957). In late 1945 a friend suggested turning that experience into a set of principles. Bill adds that such a code "could not, of course, ever become rule or law" (<2>A.A. Comes of Age</2>, 1957), but might guide the trustees, the office, and groups with growing pains. The Long Form appeared in "the Grapevine of May, 1946" (<3>A.A. Comes of Age</3>, 1957).

Comes of Age</0>, 1957); the others were that A.A. can't have a class of professional therapists and that God, speaking in the group conscience, is the final authority.
c907865e7641: None of these sources says the Traditions were written to govern an individual member's private life or recovery. That job belongs to the Steps. acd7fcd44f99: Does the Big Book endorse treatment centres?
23c114cac451: No. The words "treatment center" and "rehab" never appear in the Big Book's program text. They turn up only in some fourth-edition personal stories, as part of what those writers went through. One writer who was told to go didn't.
660039e8fb4d: The 1939 text does favor medical help in its place. It favors hospitalization for a drinker who is "very jittery or befogged" (p. xxvi). It calls physical treatment "desirable, even imperative" for someone just off a spree, but only "a small part of the picture" (p. 143). It speaks warmly of a hospital and a doctor who cooperated with A.A. (p. 162).
12b94d222264: What the book says actually recovers the alcoholic is not the medical care itself but a spiritual change and working with other alcoholics (pp. xxix, 89, 143), though for many early members that began inside a hospital's walls (p. 162).
4b92e6163231: The Traditions keep A.A. and hospitals apart. Hospitals and "other places of recuperation" are to be "well outside A.A.," and cooperation must never go so far as "affiliation or endorsement, actual or implied" (p. 564).
37fc903d4415: In the first 164 pages, the forewords and the appendices, "treatment" means a doctor's or hospital's care of a drinker. It never means a program that replaces A.A. "Treatment center" and "rehab" don't appear there at all. They appear only in personal stories in Parts II and III, which reflect the membership at the time of the fourth edition (2001). Some examples: - One writer was sent to a treatment center, and it "introduced me to the Big Book" (p. 498). - Another writes: "I didn't have anything against treatment centers then, nor do I now" (p. 315). - Another, asked to enter a treatment center, writes: "I did not go to a rehab" (p. 425). - Another remarks that when their father drank "they didn't have treatment centers" (p. 513).
5c7df84ab317: These are personal experiences, told "in his own language and from his own point of view" (p. 29). They don't make the program text say anything about treatment centres.
b3be64419925: What the 1939 text says about medical help
4ca11bf6a0a0: The Big Book isn't against doctors or hospitals. It was introduced by one, Dr. Silkworth, who ran a hospital for alcoholics (pp. xxv–xxvii). Bill W. got sober in a hospital, where "Treatment seemed wise, for I showed signs of delirium tremens" (p. 13). The text: - <0>Favors hospitalization</0> for the drinker who is very jittery or befogged, so his mind is clear before he is approached (p. xxvi). - <1>Uses doctors and hospitals to find drinkers.</1> A member can find drinkers who want to recover by asking "doctors, ministers, priests or hospitals" (p. 89). "Approach through a doctor or an institution is a better bet" than through his family (p. 91). "If your man needs hospitalization, he should have it" (p. 91). - <2>Treats physical treatment as a first step.</2> In "To Employers," for a man still drinking or just off a spree, "a certain amount of physical treatment is desirable, even imperative" (p. 143). "In competent hands, this seldom takes long nor is it very expensive" (p. 143). - <3>Thanks a hospital.</3> Chapter 11 describes "a well-known hospital for the treatment of alcoholic and drug addiction" in the East, whose doctor suggests A.A. to patients able to recover on a spiritual basis. "Many of us, former patients, go there to help" (p. 162).
7ef5a15f4691: What it says treatment can't do
56a0ce1d4225: The same pages are blunt about the limits: - "Physical treatment is but a small part of the picture." The man "must undergo a change of heart" (p. 143). - Dr. Silkworth: the craving "has never been, by any treatment with which we are familiar, permanently eradicated" (p. xxx), and doctors "have made little impression upon the problem as a whole" (p. xxix). Recovery takes "an entire psychic change" (p. xxix). - The book's own early members had tried "health farms and sanitariums" and voluntary commitment to asylums without success (p. 31). One man "floundered from one sanitarium to another" (p. 26). - The way out it offers is the Steps and Chapter 7's work. Practical experience shows, it says, that "nothing will so much insure immunity from drinking as intensive work with other alcoholics" (p. 89).

"While an A.A. group may cooperate with anyone, such cooperation ought never go so far as affiliation or endorsement, actual or implied" (p. 564). - The short form: an A.A. group "ought never endorse, finance or lend the A.A. name to any related facility or outside enterprise" (p. 562). - Tradition Eight: "We define professionalism as the occupation of counseling alcoholics for fees or hire" (p. 564), and A.A.'s Twelfth Step work is never to be paid for (pp. 564–565).
ad23dd081c1d: The Foreword to the Second Edition (1955) sums up the stance: A.A. doesn't "take any particular medical point of view, though we cooperate widely with the men of medicine" (p. xx), and "Upon therapy for the alcoholic himself, we surely have no monopoly" (p. xxi).
d449d557f44a: The Big Book doesn't endorse treatment centres. The 1939 text speaks warmly of one hospital that treated alcoholics and cooperated with A.A. (p. 162), but as a place where members went to help and found God, not as a substitute for the program; and the Traditions written after it tell A.A. groups never to endorse or affiliate with any such facility (pp. 562, 564). What the book does endorse is short, practical medical care to clear the drinker's head, followed by the spiritual program and one alcoholic working with another. It never treats a hospital stay as the recovery itself.

"The Way Out" won a close vote, until a member checked the Library of Congress and found "exactly twelve books already titled" that (P-17, "Anonymity", 1946, p. 42). Nobody wanted to be the thirteenth, so the book, and then the fellowship, became Alcoholics Anonymous (P-17, p. 42).

So the foreword asks members writing or speaking publicly about alcoholism to call themselves "a member of Alcoholics Anonymous" instead of using their names, and asks the press to respect this (p. xiii).

c076885206ae: <0>Foreword to the First Edition (1939).</0> The first paragraph states the aim: "To show other alcoholics precisely how we have recovered is the main purpose of this book." (p. xiii). (Chapter 11, p. 164).
7cc07f854751: <0>Foreword to the Second Edition (1955).</0> Looking back, it says that by late 1937 enough members had lasting sobriety to convince them "a new light had entered the dark world of the alcoholic" (p. xvii). The result was this volume, published in the spring of 1939, when membership "had then reached about 100 men and women" (p. xvii). e00300a71411: How the decision was made (later accounts)
51dc296f8d9e: <0>P-44, <1>A.A.'s Legacy of Service</1></0> (Bill W., describing events up to 1955; pamphlet © 2018). In 1937, at Dr. Bob's home in Akron, the two men added up two years' work and saw for the first time that recovery on a large scale was possible (P-44). The question was how a few recovered alcoholics could reach millions (P-44). They met with eighteen members of the Akron group; the majority wanted hospitals, paid workers and, above all, "a book for other alcoholics that could explain to them our methods and results" (P-44). The big money never came: John D. Rockefeller, Jr. gave $5,000 but declined to give more "for fear of professionalizing A.A." (P-44). Bill drafted the first two chapters in the late spring of 1938 for a fund-raising prospectus that failed, turned down a publisher's advance, and with a friend set up the fellowship's own book company, because: "It was evident that our Society ought to own and publish its own literature." (P-44). Akron, New York and Cleveland members wrote 28 stories, and the drafts were argued over for months; Bill says, "I became much more of an umpire than I ever was an author." (P-44). "The book finally appeared in April, 1939." (P-44).
9a1bca45c7c6: <0>A.A. Comes of Age (1957).</0> Bill tells the same November 1937 meeting in more detail. Word of mouth was slow, and it was also dangerous, because the message might be "garbled and twisted beyond recognition" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). "A book of experience could carry our message to distant places we could never visit ourselves." (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). It could also "prevent the otherwise inevitable garble and distortion that would start as soon as publicity came" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). The Akron meeting approved the plan only by the barest majority, and a strong minority rejected paid missionaries and hospitals; Bill later said that minority was right about those (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). The story section was finished in late January 1939 (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).

38b1d2a78ad5: <0>Chapter 2, "There Is a Solution" (1939).</0> Right after the story of the man treated by Dr. Jung, the chapter says: "The distinguished American psychologist, William James, in his book 'Varieties of Religious Experience,' indicates a multitude of ways in which men have discovered God." 3417efd60a23: How was the Big Book paid for and published (Works Publishing)?
b922fc912849: In 1938 the publisher Harper offered Bill W. an advance for the book. He and his partner Hank P. decided the fellowship should own its own book, and instead formed their own company, Works Publishing, selling $25 shares to members and friends.

b340eb874e16: The Digest article never came, and for months the book didn't sell. Publicity in 1939 and 1940 finally moved it.
58f5dcd63834: In 1940 the Alcoholic Foundation bought out the cash shareholders with money lent by Rockefeller and his friends, and Bill and Hank gave up their shares, so the Big Book came to belong to A.A. as a whole.
2b2c91303880: The 1939 text doesn't tell how it was financed. The copyright page of today's edition lists the first edition as running from 1939 to 1955, and the copyright is now held by A.A. World Services, Inc. (p. iv). The 1955 foreword says only that the members' determination "bore fruit in the spring of 1939 by the publication of this volume" (p. xvii). See <0>Why was the Big Book written, and when?</0>
fa2ed05fe98c: The decision to self-publish (1957, and P-44)
d60f85133141: In the fall of 1938, through trustee Frank Amos, Bill showed two chapters to Eugene Exman, religious editor at Harper, who offered a $1,500 advance on royalties (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Bill had second thoughts: if the book became the fellowship's main text, "Our principal written asset would then be owned by an outside publisher" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). The trustees favored Harper, but Hank P. pressed for a stock company of their own (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Exman himself agreed that a society like theirs should publish its own literature (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). P-44 (Bill, describing events through 1955) puts the reason plainly: "No publisher, however good, ought to own our best asset." (P-44).
403efde29c4f: Hank's prospectus offered 600 shares at $25: a third for cash to New York members and friends, two-thirds to Hank and Bill for their work, with the author's royalty assigned to the Foundation to soothe the trustees (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). He named the company "Since the forthcoming volume would be only the first of many such 'works,'" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957), and bought blank stock certificates at a stationery store (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).
c08a63c6d858: At first nobody bought: "What made you think that we would buy stock in a book not yet written?" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Then the managing editor of the Reader's Digest said he was almost sure the magazine would run a story when the book was ready (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). With that, "Soon we had a subscription of 200 shares which amounted to $5,000" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957), paid in installments of five dollars a month (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Charles B. Towns lent $2,500 (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957), a sum Bill elsewhere says later grew to over $4,000 (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). The money went for office costs and groceries for Bill, Lois, Hank and the secretary, Ruth Hock, until publication (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).
29b7ae92d4a6: Edward Blackwell of Cornwall Press suggested a first printing of 5,000 and accepted $500 down (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). They set the price at $3.50 after heated argument, and to give buyers their money's worth used the thickest paper in the shop: "The original volume proved to be so bulky that it became known as the 'Big Book.'" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).
aa05009e96bb: When Bill and Hank went back to the Reader's Digest, the editor had forgotten them; his staff had turned the idea down (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). "The book enterprise had collapsed." (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Twenty-eight copies were owed to the story writers and forty-nine to subscribers (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Blackwell stood by them (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). A radio appearance and 20,000 postcards to doctors brought two orders (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). An A.A. tailor, Bert T., borrowed $1,000 against his own business to keep the company going (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Sales began with a Liberty magazine article in September 1939 (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957), and grew after Rockefeller's dinner in 1940 (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).
